extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and researchers of television comedy and producers of roast-style specials
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines, recurring practices, and production/content norms for Comedy Central's celebrity roast television specials, including format, participant roles, editing practices, and notable content limits. Useful for understanding how these roast specials are structured and produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series format and basic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy Central Roast is a series of celebrity roast specials that air on the American television channel Comedy Central. Eight to ten people are invited, and they each roast one another before finally roasting the titular subject of the roast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes the canonical structure: a group of roasters (often including a roastmaster), individual sets where roasters make jokes about each other, and then the collective focusing on the honoree/roastee. Pre-taped appearances and surprise guests are commonly incorporated into this structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical running time
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most Comedy Central Roast specials are produced to fill a roughly 90-minute telecast window (this is the stated running time for the series).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of roasters/participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Eight to ten people are invited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly lists roasters per roast and indicates the typical size of the roaster panel; roasts often include a roastmaster plus several roasters, pre-taped contributors, surprise guests, and notable audience members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roastmaster role and recurring performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Roastmaster(s) lead the event; some individuals serve repeatedly in this role (e.g., Seth MacFarlane is noted as the most frequent roastmaster with three turns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The roastmaster organizes/hosts the evening; the page documents recurring roasters and roastmasters (Jeff Ross appearing most frequently as a roaster, Seth MacFarlane recurring as roastmaster), implying production preference for familiar hosts/regulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content limits / off-limits topics (roastee requests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some roastees have stated that certain topics are off limits. Pamela Anderson, for example, prohibited jokes about her Hepatitis C infection. Joan Rivers disallowed jokes about her daughter Melissa, William Shatner asked that the death of his wife not be mentioned, and Donald Trump prohibited jokes about him not being as wealthy as he claims he is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roastees may set boundaries in advance; these requests are sometimes respected in taping and/or post-production. The page also notes that other roastees (e.g., David Hasselhoff) have imposed no limits, so practices vary per subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing / broadcast censorship and post-production cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes and segments are sometimes removed from the official broadcast. Examples: a Steve-O joke referencing The Station nightclub fire was removed from broadcast on his request; multiple jokes about Paul Walker were cut from the Justin Bieber roast broadcast; other jokes were cut from broadcasts at the network's or performers' request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roasts are taped and edited before airing; material that appears in taping may be omitted from the televised version (or restored on DVDs). Editing decisions can be driven by performer requests, legal or sensitivity concerns, audience reaction, or network standards. The page also cites instances where DVD releases differ from TV versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content tone and acceptable comedic approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Roast humor typically includes racy, sexual, and highly personal jokes directed at the roastee and fellow roasters. However, tone can vary: Norm Macdonald's set 'avoided racy content and featured intentionally cheesy and antiquated jokes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and performers may choose a spectrum from 'shocking' to intentionally tame material; audience reaction and editing can reflect these choices. The page provides examples of both extremes and the resulting critical/audience responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-taped segments, surprise appearances, and musical/visual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts often include pre-taped appearances by celebrities, surprise guest performances, montages, and musical numbers (e.g., pre-taped appearances by Michael J. Fox, Conan O'Brien; musical parodies or montages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These production elements are regular features used to vary pacing and add production value. The page notes that some pre-taped content can be restored to DVD releases or omitted from TV broadcasts for rights or editorial reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/rights constraints on included material
rubrics_metrics.description: For legal reasons, certain clips may not be used in broadcasts (example: clips of Charlie Sheen's tenure on Two and a Half Men were never used in a montage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights clearance and legal constraints affect what archival footage, clips, or songs can appear in the televised roast; replacements (e.g., instrumentals) may be used on DVD or broadcast if licensing isn't available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling, cancellation and location conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts can be announced, rescheduled, or cancelled; example: a roast for Willie Nelson was planned but ultimately cancelled; Kid Rock's roast was announced and later replaced. Kid Rock conditioned his roast on it being filmed in Detroit, which Comedy Central refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistical demands from participants (preferred city/venue), network scheduling priorities, and other production considerations can lead to cancellation or rescheduling. Negotiations about location can determine whether an announced roast proceeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: International production and localization
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2010, Comedy Central affiliates outside the United States have occasionally produced their own roasts; twelve such roasts have aired so far, in five countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International affiliates adapt the roast format for local personalities and cultural contexts (different roastmasters, roastees, and regional sensitivity norms are documented in the page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue selection and common filming locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple roasts have been filmed at recurring venues; as of the Alec Baldwin roast, Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City, California has hosted the most roasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers often favor particular studios or large performance venues for taping; venue choice can be a recurring production element (studio availability, geographic convenience, and stage capabilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reception and ratings as success metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The page regularly lists US viewership numbers (millions) for each roast and calls Denis Leary's roast 'the most watched program in the channel's history' (excluding South Park).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratings/viewership are tracked per roast and cited as indicators of success; producers and network decisions (e.g., whether to produce more roasts) are influenced by these metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and industry recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Roasts may be eligible for awards and nominations (example: the Roast of William Shatner was nominated for a 2007 Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Variety Special).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical recognition (award nominations) is a documented outcome for some roasts and can factor into perceptions of prestige or quality.
